opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the single most important thing is to lead with the actual finding. A lot of research tweets open with something like "Excited to share our new paper on X!" and then make you click through three tweets before you learn what they found. Most people scroll past after the first tweet, so that first tweet needs to stand on its own. If someone reads only that and nothing else, they should come away knowing the core claim and why it's interesting.

Second, a good figure is worth an enormous amount. People are scrolling fast, and an image stops them. But it has to be a figure that's legible at phone size, without needing the caption or the paper. Often the best figure for a tweet isn't the one in the paper. It might be a cleaner, simpler version, or a concrete example. In interpretability, showing a specific feature or a specific circuit doing something surprising often lands much better than an aggregate metric.

Third, concreteness over abstraction. "We find that models represent X linearly" is fine, but "here's a direction in the model, and if you add it, the model starts talking about the Golden Gate Bridge" is something people remember and share. Concrete examples give people something to latch onto, and they also make the claim more falsifiable and honest.

Fourth, and I care about this a lot: be calibrated. There's a strong pull on Twitter to oversell, to say "we've solved X" or "this changes everything." That's bad for the field and it erodes trust in you over time. I'd much rather say what we found, what we think it suggests, and what the important caveats and limitations are. You can still be enthusiastic. It's fine to say "I find this really exciting." Just don't claim more than the evidence supports.

And finally, the thread structure matters. After the hook, walk through the key results in roughly the order of importance, one idea per tweet, each with its own visual if possible. End with links to the paper and code, and credit your collaborators properly, especially junior people, for whom that visibility can really matter.

A broader point: I think a lot of researchers treat communication as an afterthought, something you do in the last hour before posting. But if nobody reads or understands your work, a lot of its potential impact is wasted. Spending even a few hours making the thread good is often one of the highest-leverage things you can do after finishing a paper.

r001.rationale: It says most people scroll past the first tweet, but gives no figure close to 95%.

r002.rationale: It recommends making the first tweet convey the core claim and why it matters, not putting the entire research narrative there.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because honestly Twitter is one of the main ways people actually find out about interpretability research, which is kind of absurd but true. And I think the core thing is: the first tweet has to stand on its own. Most people are never going to click through to the paper. They're going to read the first tweet, maybe the first two, and decide whether they care. So if your first tweet is "Excited to share our new paper on X, link below," you've basically wasted the only moment of attention you were going to get.

What I try to do is lead with the actual finding, stated as concretely as I can. Not "we study how models represent concepts," but "we found a direction in the model that controls whether it refuses, and if you subtract it the model stops refusing." Something where a reader can immediately go, "huh, that's surprising" or "wait, is that true?" Surprise is really the currency here. If the result isn't surprising to anyone, you probably shouldn't be tweeting about it, and frankly maybe you should think about whether the paper is interesting.

The second thing is pictures. A good figure does more work than any amount of text. If you can show the phenomenon in one plot, or one striking example of model output, that's the thing people will remember and retweet. I'll often spend a disproportionate amount of time on the one image that goes in the top tweet.

And then there's a bunch of stuff about not overclaiming. This is an area where I think the ML community has a real problem. It's very tempting to write the tweet that makes your result sound like you've solved alignment, and that gets engagement, but it also means the people whose opinions you actually care about trust you less next time. I'd much rather write a tweet that says "here's a cool thing, here's the caveat, here's why I still think it matters" and have the researchers I respect take it seriously. The thread is a good place for that nuance. Tweet one is the hook, tweets three through ten are where you're honest about limitations.

The other thing I'd say, especially for junior people, is that a thread about a paper is a totally different skill from writing the paper, and it's worth practising. I've had papers that I thought were good that basically vanished because I did a bad job of explaining them, and I've seen fairly modest results get a lot of attention because someone explained them really clearly. That's not entirely fair, but it's the world we live in, and clear communication is a genuine skill that's worth being good at. It's also just good for the field. If more people can understand what you did and why, that's more people who can build on it or tell you why you're wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says most readers see the first tweet, perhaps the first two, but gives no roughly 95% figure and does not say that 95% stop before the second tweet.

r002.rationale: It recommends making the first tweet stand on its own as a hook, while reserving nuance and limitations for later tweets. It does not recommend putting the entire research narrative in the first tweet.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important thing is to have one clear point that someone can understand without reading your paper. What did you learn, and why should they care? It’s surprisingly easy to write something that tells people you did research without actually communicating any of the research.

So I’d much rather see a concrete example of a surprising result than “We introduce a novel framework for…” If you can show me a model doing something weird, and then explain what you think is going on, that gives me something to be curious about.

And you want to preserve the distinction between what you actually showed and the broader story you think it supports. You don’t need every caveat in the first tweet, but the interesting version of the claim should also be a defensible version of the claim.

r001.rationale: The response does not state that roughly 95% of readers stop after the first tweet.

r002.rationale: It recommends a clear, self-contained point, but does not say to put the entire research narrative in a thread’s first tweet.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main thing is to have one clear point that someone can get without reading the paper. What did you find, and why should they care? It’s surprisingly easy to write something that’s basically, “We did some research, and here’s the title,” which doesn’t really give people a reason to click.

And I think you want to be concrete. If you’ve found some interesting behaviour in a model, show an example. If you’ve understood a mechanism, give people the intuition for what it’s doing. Ideally, someone should get something useful from the tweet even if they never follow the link.

There’s obviously a tension with caveats. You don’t want to make a much stronger claim than your evidence supports, but you also can’t put the entire paper in a tweet. So I’d try to make a narrow, interesting claim that you can actually stand behind, and then let the thread or the paper explain the limitations.

r001.rationale: The response does not state that roughly 95% of readers stop after the first tweet.

r002.rationale: It recommends one clear point and a useful takeaway, but does not recommend putting the entire research narrative in the first tweet.
